questions.stem: Breadth-first graph search runs on the undirected graph in the figure from $S$ to $G$. Successors are generated in alphabetical order, a node already in the frontier or already expanded is not added again, and the goal test is applied when a node is selected for expansion. In which order are nodes expanded (the goal counts as expanded)?
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 335 180" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" fill="currentColor"><path d="M35 84L85 51M35 96L85 129M106 41L159 24M105 51L160 84M105 129L160 96M106 139L159 156M181 25L299 85M181 155L299 95M298 90L257 90M182 90L233 90" fill="none" stroke="currentColor"/><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor"><circle cx="25" cy="90" r="12"/><circle cx="95" cy="45" r="12"/><circle cx="95" cy="135" r="12"/><circle cx="170" cy="20" r="12"/><circle cx="170" cy="90" r="12"/><circle cx="170" cy="160" r="12"/><circle cx="245" cy="90" r="12"/><circle cx="310" cy="90" r="12"/></g><g text-anchor="middle"><text x="25" y="94">S</text><text x="95" y="49">B</text><text x="95" y="139">D</text><text x="170" y="24">A</text><text x="170" y="94">C</text><text x="170" y="164">F</text><text x="245" y="94">G</text><text x="310" y="94">E</text></g></svg>

options.text: S, B, A, E, F, D, C, G
options.why: This is the depth-first order: it dives B → A → E before finishing level 1.

options.text: S, B, D, A, C, E, F, G
options.why: Sorted the third level alphabetically; BFS keeps FIFO order, and F (added by D) was queued before E (added by A).

options.text: S, B, D, A, C, F, E, G
options.why: Queue: S adds B, D; B adds A, C; D adds F; A adds E; C adds G. G is dequeued last.

options.text: S, B, C, G
options.why: This is the returned path S–B–C–G, not the expansion order.

questions.solution:
1. Expand S: queue B, D.
2. B: add A, C. D: C is already queued, add F. Queue A, C, F.
3. A: add E. C: add G. Queue F, E, G.
4. F and E add nothing new; G is dequeued and passes the test. Order: S, B, D, A, C, F, E, G.

questions.stem:
Two depth-first searches run on the graph in the figure from $S$ to $G$. Both skip visited nodes, stop as soon as $G$ is visited, and return the path through the parent each node was reached from.

- **Recursive DFS:** from the current node, recurse into the unvisited neighbours in alphabetical order.
- **Stack DFS:** pop a node; if it is already visited, skip it; otherwise mark it visited (stop if it is $G$) and push all its unvisited neighbours in alphabetical order, so the alphabetically last one is popped next.

Which statements are correct?
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 335 180" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" fill="currentColor"><path d="M35 84L85 51M35 96L85 129M106 41L159 24M105 51L160 84M105 129L160 96M106 139L159 156M181 25L299 85M181 155L299 95M298 90L257 90M182 90L233 90" fill="none" stroke="currentColor"/><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor"><circle cx="25" cy="90" r="12"/><circle cx="95" cy="45" r="12"/><circle cx="95" cy="135" r="12"/><circle cx="170" cy="20" r="12"/><circle cx="170" cy="90" r="12"/><circle cx="170" cy="160" r="12"/><circle cx="245" cy="90" r="12"/><circle cx="310" cy="90" r="12"/></g><g text-anchor="middle"><text x="25" y="94">S</text><text x="95" y="49">B</text><text x="95" y="139">D</text><text x="170" y="24">A</text><text x="170" y="94">C</text><text x="170" y="164">F</text><text x="245" y="94">G</text><text x="310" y="94">E</text></g></svg>

options.text: Recursive DFS visits all 8 nodes and returns the path S–B–A–E–F–D–C–G
options.why: Each call takes the first unvisited neighbour: S → B → A → E → F → D → C → G, snaking through every node.

options.text: Stack DFS returns the path S–D–F–E–G
options.why: Pop S, push B, D; pop D, push C, F; pop F, push E; pop E, push A, G; pop G.

options.text: Recursive DFS returns the same path as BFS, S–B–C–G
options.why: DFS does not look for the fewest edges; at B it takes A first (alphabetical) and dives deep.

options.text: Both searches visit the nodes in the same order
options.why: Pushing in alphabetical order makes the stack pop the **last** neighbour first, so stack DFS goes S, D, … while recursive DFS goes S, B, …

questions.solution:
1. Recursive: S → B (first neighbour) → A → E → F → D → C → G; the path has 7 edges.
2. Stack: pop S, push B, D. Pop D, push C, F. Pop F, push E. Pop E, push A, G. Pop G: path S–D–F–E–G.
3. BFS would return S–B–C–G (3 edges).

questions.stem: Breadth-first graph search runs on the graph in the figure from $S$ to $G$, generating successors alphabetically and never re-adding a node that is already in the frontier or expanded. Let $n_1$ be the number of nodes **removed from the frontier** when the goal test is applied on expansion (removing $G$ itself counts), and $n_2$ the number removed when the goal test is applied on generation (the search stops the moment $G$ is generated). Find $n_1-n_2$.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 335 180" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" fill="currentColor"><path d="M35 84L85 51M35 96L85 129M106 41L159 24M105 51L160 84M105 129L160 96M106 139L159 156M181 25L299 85M181 155L299 95M298 90L257 90M182 90L233 90" fill="none" stroke="currentColor"/><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor"><circle cx="25" cy="90" r="12"/><circle cx="95" cy="45" r="12"/><circle cx="95" cy="135" r="12"/><circle cx="170" cy="20" r="12"/><circle cx="170" cy="90" r="12"/><circle cx="170" cy="160" r="12"/><circle cx="245" cy="90" r="12"/><circle cx="310" cy="90" r="12"/></g><g text-anchor="middle"><text x="25" y="94">S</text><text x="95" y="49">B</text><text x="95" y="139">D</text><text x="170" y="24">A</text><text x="170" y="94">C</text><text x="170" y="164">F</text><text x="245" y="94">G</text><text x="310" y="94">E</text></g></svg>

traps.why: Did not count the removal of $G$ itself in $n_1$ ($7-5$).
Gave $n_1$ alone instead of the difference.
Gave $n_2$ alone instead of the difference.

questions.solution:
1. Test on expansion: removals S, B, D, A, C, F, E, G, so $n_1=8$.
2. Test on generation: G is generated while C is expanded; removals S, B, D, A, C, so $n_2=5$.
3. $n_1-n_2=3$.

questions.stem: BFS runs on a complete tree with branching factor 3; expanding a node generates all 3 of its children at once. The only goal is the **leftmost** node at depth 2. With the goal test applied **when a node is generated**, how many nodes have been generated (counting the root) when the search stops?

options.why: Stopped halfway through an expansion; the stem says all 3 children are generated at once.
This is the count with the goal test on expansion: all depth-1 nodes are expanded before the goal is popped ($1+3+9$).
Stopped after expanding the root; a depth-2 goal appears only when a depth-1 node is expanded.
Root, its 3 children, and the 3 children of the first depth-1 node, which include the goal.

questions.solution:
1. Root generated: 1.
2. Expand the root: 3 children, total 4.
3. Expand the leftmost depth-1 node: its 3 children (one is the goal) are generated, total 7, and the test on generation stops the search.
4. With the test on expansion all three depth-1 nodes would be expanded first: $1+3+9=13$.

questions.stem: Uniform-cost graph search runs on the weighted undirected graph in the figure from $S$ to $G$. A frontier node's cost is lowered when a cheaper path is found, ties are broken alphabetically, and the goal test is applied when a node is popped. Which statements are correct?
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 325 180" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" fill="currentColor"><path d="M34 83L91 37M34 97L91 143M100 42L100 138M110 143L180 97M110 37L180 83M112 150L258 150M200 97L260 143M201 84L289 36M273 138L297 42" fill="none" stroke="currentColor"/><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor"><circle cx="25" cy="90" r="12"/><circle cx="100" cy="30" r="12"/><circle cx="100" cy="150" r="12"/><circle cx="190" cy="90" r="12"/><circle cx="270" cy="150" r="12"/><circle cx="300" cy="30" r="12"/></g><g text-anchor="middle"><text x="25" y="94">S</text><text x="100" y="34">A</text><text x="100" y="154">B</text><text x="190" y="94">C</text><text x="270" y="154">D</text><text x="300" y="34">G</text><text x="55" y="55">5</text><text x="55" y="134">2</text><text x="90" y="94">2</text><text x="156" y="133">6</text><text x="150" y="52">2</text><text x="185" y="166">9</text><text x="240" y="113">1</text><text x="240" y="52">6</text><text x="297" y="95">4</text></g></svg>

options.text: Before $G$ is popped, the nodes are expanded in the order S, B, A, C, D
$A$ is expanded with $g(A)=5$
options.why: Kept A's first cost from the edge S–A; expanding B lowers it to $2+2=4$.

options.text: The returned path is S–B–A–C–D–G, with cost 11
options.why: $2+2+2+1+4=11$; the route ending with C–G costs 12.

options.text: The search stops when $G$ is first generated, with cost 12
options.why: G is generated with $g=12$ while C is expanded, but UCS stops only when G is popped; D lowers it to 11 first.

questions.stem: For the graph in the figure, uniform-cost search runs from $S$ to $G$ (goal test on pop, frontier costs lowered when a cheaper path appears, ties alphabetical). What is $g(D)$ at the moment $D$ is expanded?
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 325 180" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" fill="currentColor"><path d="M34 83L91 37M34 97L91 143M100 42L100 138M110 143L180 97M110 37L180 83M112 150L258 150M200 97L260 143M201 84L289 36M273 138L297 42" fill="none" stroke="currentColor"/><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor"><circle cx="25" cy="90" r="12"/><circle cx="100" cy="30" r="12"/><circle cx="100" cy="150" r="12"/><circle cx="190" cy="90" r="12"/><circle cx="270" cy="150" r="12"/><circle cx="300" cy="30" r="12"/></g><g text-anchor="middle"><text x="25" y="94">S</text><text x="100" y="34">A</text><text x="100" y="154">B</text><text x="190" y="94">C</text><text x="270" y="154">D</text><text x="300" y="34">G</text><text x="55" y="55">5</text><text x="55" y="134">2</text><text x="90" y="94">2</text><text x="156" y="133">6</text><text x="150" y="52">2</text><text x="185" y="166">9</text><text x="240" y="113">1</text><text x="240" y="52">6</text><text x="297" y="95">4</text></g></svg>

traps.why: Kept D's first cost via S–B–D ($2+9$) and never lowered it.
Used the last edge weight C–D instead of the total path cost.
Went S–A–C–D ($5+2+1$), missing that A is cheaper via B.
Went S–B–C–D ($2+6+1$), missing the cheaper route to C through A.

questions.solution:
1. Cheapest costs: B=2, A=4 (via B), C=6 (via A).
2. D is first reached from B with $2+9=11$, then lowered to $6+1=7$ when C is expanded.
3. D is popped with $g(D)=7$.

questions.stem: Iterative deepening search runs on the tree in the figure with depth limits $0,1,2,\dots$; children are visited left to right and the goal test is applied when a node is visited. The goal is $H$. Counting every visit in every iteration (the root counts each time), how many node visits are made in total?
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 320 175" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12" fill="currentColor"><path d="M150 23L70 60M160 29L160 54M170 23L250 60M54 74L36 103M66 74L84 103M160 76L160 101M254 74L236 103M266 74L284 103M30 123L30 148" fill="none" stroke="currentColor"/><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor"><circle cx="160" cy="18" r="11"/><circle cx="60" cy="65" r="11"/><circle cx="160" cy="65" r="11"/><circle cx="260" cy="65" r="11"/><circle cx="30" cy="112" r="11"/><circle cx="90" cy="112" r="11"/><circle cx="160" cy="112" r="11"/><circle cx="230" cy="112" r="11"/><circle cx="290" cy="112" r="11"/><circle cx="30" cy="159" r="11"/></g><g text-anchor="middle"><text x="160" y="22">A</text><text x="60" y="69">B</text><text x="160" y="69">C</text><text x="260" y="69">D</text><text x="30" y="116">E</text><text x="90" y="116">F</text><text x="160" y="116">G</text><text x="230" y="116">H</text><text x="290" y="116">I</text><text x="30" y="163">J</text></g></svg>

traps.why: Forgot the limit-0 iteration, which visits A once.
Ran the last iteration to the end and counted I too; the search stops at H.

questions.solution:
1. Limit 0: A (1 visit).
2. Limit 1: A, B, C, D (4).
3. Limit 2: A, B, E, F, C, G, D, H, stopping at H (8).
4. Total $1+4+8=13$.

questions.stem: Iterative deepening search (limits $0,1,2,\dots$) runs on a tree whose shallowest goal is the **last** node at depth 3, so every iteration runs to completion. How many times in total is a particular node at depth 1 visited?

options.why: That is the root's count ($d+1$); a depth-1 node is not visited in the limit-0 iteration.
IDS keeps nothing between iterations, so shallow nodes are visited again in every deeper iteration.
It is visited once in each iteration with limit 1, 2 and 3: $d-i+1=3-1+1$.
Left out the final iteration with limit 3, which also passes through depth 1.

questions.solution:
1. A node at depth $i$ is visited in every iteration with limit $\ell\ge i$.
2. Limits run $0,1,2,3$, so a depth-1 node is visited for $\ell=1,2,3$: 3 times.
3. In general it is $d-i+1$ times; the root ($i=0$) gets $d+1$.

questions.stem: A finite graph has cycles, and its step costs are positive but unequal (some edges cost 1, others 10). Which statements are correct?

options.text: UCS with the goal test on pop returns a cheapest path
options.why: Step costs are $\ge1>0$, so UCS is complete and optimal when it tests the goal on pop.

options.text: BFS returns a cheapest path because it finds the shallowest goal
options.why: Fewest edges is cheapest only when all step costs are equal; one edge of cost 10 loses to three edges of cost 1.

options.text: Graph-search DFS (with a visited set) is guaranteed to terminate
options.why: With a visited set, each of the finitely many nodes is expanded at most once.

options.text: Tree-search DFS (no visited set) is complete on this graph
options.why: Without a visited set, DFS can circle a cycle forever, even on a finite graph.

questions.solution:
1. UCS: every cost is $\ge\varepsilon=1>0$ and the goal is tested on pop, so it is complete and optimal.
2. Graph-search DFS: finite graph plus a visited set, so it terminates (but it is not optimal).
3. BFS minimises the number of edges, not the total cost.
4. Tree-search DFS can go round a cycle forever.

questions.stem: Depth-limited search with limit $\ell=3$ runs on a problem with finite branching factor whose shallowest goal is at depth 5. What happens?

options.text: It returns failure (cutoff) without finding a goal
options.why: Nodes deeper than 3 are never generated and no goal lies within depth 3, so DLS is incomplete when $\ell<d$.

options.text: It finds the goal at depth 5, but the path may not be optimal
options.why: The limit is a hard cut: nodes below depth 3 are never generated, so depth 5 is never reached.

options.text: It loops forever because the goal is never found
options.why: With finite $b$ and a depth cut, the search space is finite, so DLS always terminates.

options.text: It returns a node at depth 3 as the goal
options.why: Reaching the limit is not reaching a goal; the goal test fails on every node within depth 3.

questions.solution:
1. DLS treats nodes at depth $\ell=3$ as leaves.
2. The shallowest goal is at depth $5>3$, so no goal is ever generated.
3. The finite tree up to depth 3 is exhausted and DLS reports cutoff/failure: it is incomplete when $\ell<d$.

questions.stem: The worst-case number of nodes generated by uniform-cost search is bounded by $b^{1+\lfloor C^*/\varepsilon\rfloor}$. Evaluate this bound for $b=2$, optimal cost $C^*=14$ and minimum step cost $\varepsilon=3$.

traps.why: Rounded $14/3$ up to 5 instead of taking the floor.
Multiplied instead of raising to a power: $b\,(1+\lfloor C^*/\varepsilon\rfloor)$, a DFS-style $bm$ formula.

questions.stem: A search tree has branching factor $b=2$, shallowest goal depth $d=10$ and maximum depth $m=20$. Using the standard worst-case **space** orders, which estimate of the number of nodes held in memory is right?

options.text: BFS $\approx1024$, IDS $\approx1024$, DFS $\approx40$
options.why: Gave IDS the BFS memory; IDS is a DFS underneath and stores only $O(bd)$.

options.text: BFS $\approx1024$, IDS $\approx20$, DFS $\approx2^{20}\approx10^6$
options.why: Used the DFS **time** $b^m$ as its space; DFS stores only the current path and siblings, $O(bm)$.

options.text: BFS $\approx20$, IDS $\approx20$, DFS $\approx40$
options.why: Gave BFS linear memory; BFS must hold a whole level of the tree, $O(b^d)$.

options.text: BFS $\approx1024$, IDS $\approx20$, DFS $\approx40$
options.why: Space: BFS $b^d=2^{10}$, IDS $bd=2\cdot10$, DFS $bm=2\cdot20$.

questions.solution:
1. BFS keeps a whole frontier level: $O(b^d)=2^{10}=1024$.
2. IDS is depth-first inside: $O(bd)=2\cdot10=20$.
3. DFS: $O(bm)=2\cdot20=40$ (its **time** is $O(b^m)$).
